paragraphs: This paper studies how a system can learn visual concepts and identify the corresponding regions in three dimensions using RGBD images and paired questions and answers. Many visual reasoning systems first depend on supervised two-dimensional segmentation. The authors instead connect language directly to a continuous representation of the underlying scene.

Their representation assigns a high-dimensional descriptor to each three-dimensional coordinate. Comparing that descriptor with an embedding of a language concept indicates how strongly the location matches the concept. Because neural fields are continuous and differentiable, the system can learn concepts and segmentation together. Operators such as filtering and counting connect these representations to question answering, allowing semantic categories and individual object regions to emerge from question-answer supervision.

Experiments report better semantic and instance segmentation than the evaluated unsupervised and language-mediated segmentation models, alongside improved three-dimensional visual reasoning. The framework also generalizes to unseen shape categories and real scans. These findings support learning spatial concepts through reasoning supervision, without first requiring the supervised two-dimensional masks used by the approaches described in the abstract.
neurips-2022-3d-concept-grounding-on-neu.tldr: A continuous neural-field representation learns three-dimensional concepts and object segmentations from question-answer supervision.

paragraphs: The paper studies online optimization when an algorithm can evaluate a function but cannot directly obtain its gradient. The functions are assumed to be convex and Lipschitz, meaning their values change at a bounded rate. The central contribution is a gradient estimator that uses two function evaluations and a random direction drawn from the l1 sphere.

The authors insert this estimator into online dual averaging and analyze different combinations of feasible-set geometry and Lipschitz assumptions. They also consider two noise models: canceling noise and adversarial noise. Their algorithm is anytime and fully data-driven, adapting to the problem parameters instead of requiring them to be specified beforehand.

For the canceling-noise setting, the resulting guarantees match or improve on the cited leading bounds for non-adaptive algorithms. The proof develops a weighted Poincaré-type inequality with explicit constants for the uniform distribution on the l1 sphere. This mathematical result supports the estimator analysis and may also be useful independently. The contribution therefore combines an adaptive optimization procedure with a new tool for understanding its randomized estimates.
neurips-2022-a-gradient-estimator-via-l1.tldr: A two-evaluation gradient estimator enables adaptive online optimization with competitive guarantees under canceling noise.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning estimates value functions for policy evaluation. This paper examines a regularized, non-parametric version of TD(0), asking how its estimates converge as observations accumulate. It treats both independent observations and Markovian observations, so the analysis includes data whose successive samples are linked through a state-transition process.

The method represents value estimates in a universal reproducing kernel Hilbert space, or RKHS. The main result proves convergence of averaged iterates to the target value function even when that function is not itself an element of the RKHS. This distinction matters: the convergence claim does not require the exact target to belong to the space used to represent the individual estimates.

The authors also provide explicit convergence rates. Those rates depend on a source condition connecting the target function's regularity to the chosen RKHS, making that relationship part of the guarantee. A numerical example on a simple continuous-state Markov reward process illustrates the convergence. Together, the results describe both eventual convergence and how quickly finite sequences of estimates approach the target under the stated conditions.
neurips-2022-a-non-asymptotic-analysis-o.tldr: Regularized kernel TD(0) receives explicit convergence guarantees, including when the target value function lies outside its RKHS.

paragraphs: Sparse rewards make reinforcement learning difficult because an agent receives limited feedback about useful behavior. Demonstrations can help supply that guidance, including examples from the target task and somewhat related activities. This paper asks how to make better use of demonstrations by combining two ways of storing the knowledge they provide.

An implicit prior compresses demonstrations into a learned model, while an explicit prior keeps information in a database that can be queried. CEIP combines these approaches. It runs multiple implicit priors, represented by normalizing flows, in parallel to construct a more complex prior. An explicit retrieval and push-forward mechanism then conditions those implicit priors, connecting the stored examples to the learned guidance.

The authors evaluate CEIP in three challenging environments and report improvements over sophisticated state-of-the-art techniques. The findings support combining retrieved demonstrations with multiple learned priors for the tested tasks. The contribution is specifically a way to organize and use available demonstration knowledge when sparse rewards make learning from interaction alone difficult.
neurips-2022-ceip-combining-explicit-and.tldr: CEIP improves reinforcement learning with demonstrations by combining retrievable examples with multiple learned priors.

paragraphs: CLEVRER-Humans is a video reasoning benchmark designed to evaluate judgments about physical events and their causes using human labels. The authors identify two problems with benchmarks built entirely from synthetic events and descriptions: limited diversity and causal relationships determined by rules that may disagree with human judgments.

The dataset introduces Causal Event Graphs as a representation of events in videos. To collect these efficiently, the authors use an iterative event cloze task that elicits the graph representation. They also use neural language generation for data augmentation. The collected graphs are then converted into questions and answers, keeping the evaluation format consistent with earlier work.

The paper evaluates a collection of baseline approaches and finds that the benchmark presents substantial challenges. Its main contribution is an evaluation resource that brings human causal judgments and descriptions into physical video reasoning. That matters because success on mechanically generated questions may not capture the same abilities as answering questions grounded in how people describe events and interpret their causal relationships.
neurips-2022-clevrer-humans-describing-p.tldr: CLEVRER-Humans introduces a challenging video reasoning benchmark grounded in human descriptions and judgments of physical causes.

paragraphs: A classifier's vocabulary can become more detailed over time: an earlier label such as dog may later be divided into individual breeds. This paper formalizes that situation through Learning with Evolving Class Ontology, or LECO. Each time period introduces finer labels that refine the categories available in previous periods.

The protocol examines practical choices about handling these changes. Should developers relabel existing examples or annotate new ones? How should older coarse labels be used? Should the previous model be fine-tuned or replaced by one trained from scratch? The authors investigate these questions through image classification on CIFAR and iNaturalist and semantic segmentation on Mapillary.

Their experiments find that labeling new data with the updated vocabulary is substantially better than relabeling the existing dataset. This leaves a mixture of old coarse labels and new fine labels. Methods adapted from semi-supervised and partial-label learning handle that inconsistency effectively, approaching an oracle trained on the combined data fully relabeled with the newest vocabulary. The result supports expanding annotated data while retaining useful information from older labels.
neurips-2022-continual-learning-with-evo.tldr: When categories become finer, LECO experiments favor labeling new data and learning jointly from old coarse and new fine labels.

paragraphs: Deep metric learning places examples in an embedding space where semantically similar items should be close together. Errors arise when similar examples end up far apart or dissimilar examples appear close. This paper introduces an empirical influence function, EIF, to trace these errors back to the training data.

EIF identifies and quantifies how subsets of training examples contribute to a model's generalization errors. This gives developers a way to investigate a particular failure through the examples that influenced it. For a user-specified error, the method can also guide relabeling of a potentially noisy training example as a mitigation.

In the quantitative evaluation, EIF identifies more relevant training samples than the traditional baseline with statistical significance, while taking 33.5% less time. A field study reports labeling mistakes of 4.4%, 6.6%, and 17.7% on CUB200, CARS196, and InShop, respectively. These findings show that the method can support both model debugging and dataset inspection. Its explanations connect embedding failures to actionable training-data issues rather than merely describing where the embedding went wrong.
neurips-2022-debugging-and-explaining-me.tldr: EIF traces metric-learning errors to influential training examples, helping identify mislabeled data and guide corrections.

paragraphs: Video-language pretraining learns representations that can transfer to tasks involving both video and text. This paper focuses on first-person video, whereas the strongest prior systems described in the abstract rely on large third-person datasets. It develops data, a training objective, and a development benchmark specifically for the egocentric setting.

EgoClip contains 3.8 million clip-text pairs selected from Ego4D and covers varied everyday human activities. The proposed EgoNCE objective adapts contrastive video-text learning by choosing positive and negative samples with the egocentric domain in mind. EgoMCQ provides a nearby development benchmark, helping the authors validate and explore decisions about the dataset and training objective efficiently.

The resulting pretraining shows strong performance on five downstream tasks across three datasets. These include video-text retrieval on EPIC-KITCHENS-100, action recognition on Charades-Ego, and natural-language queries, moment queries, and object-state-change classification on Ego4D benchmarks. Together, these results support the usefulness of first-person-specific pretraining across several kinds of egocentric understanding, from matching descriptions to video through recognizing actions and changes in objects.
neurips-2022-egocentric-video-language-p.tldr: EgoClip, EgoNCE, and EgoMCQ support first-person video-language pretraining with strong results across five downstream tasks.

paragraphs: Evaluating a graph generator requires a meaningful way to compare collections of graphs. Existing techniques described in this paper either count graph substructures or use representations produced by randomly initialized graph neural networks. The authors investigate whether learning those representations can make the resulting evaluation metrics more reliable.

Their proposed approach uses features from graph neural networks trained with a contrastive objective. They find that these learned features provide more reliable metrics than features from random networks. However, the comparison with traditional subgraph-counting approaches reveals an important qualification: neither family dominates the other. The paper gives examples of graphs that each approach fails to distinguish.

The authors then examine Graph Substructure Networks, which combine aspects of substructure-based and neural approaches. These networks better distinguish distances between graph datasets in the reported study. The overall finding favors learned representations while also showing why representation choice matters: a metric can miss structural differences that another metric detects. Combining complementary sources of structural information offers a stronger basis for the evaluated comparisons.
neurips-2022-evaluating-graph-generative.tldr: Contrastively learned graph features improve generator evaluation, while combining neural and substructure information helps address complementary blind spots.

paragraphs: This paper approaches explainability as a practical design problem: explanations must meet the ambitions of explainable AI while fitting the constraints of deep learning. The authors define a set of desiderata covering both concerns and propose training a system to construct a causal model of itself as a way to satisfy them.

For deep reinforcement learning agents, they instantiate this idea as Causal Self-Talk. The agent learns to communicate with itself across time. This learned communication is the basis of a model that supports explanations of the agent's own behavior. The approach therefore makes learning an explanatory model part of the agent's training process.

In a simulated three-dimensional environment, the authors demonstrate faithful explanations with meaningful semantic content. They also show that the learned models can support semantic control interfaces, giving the approach a role beyond explaining completed behavior. The stated results connect explanation and control through an agent's learned causal model of itself, with the demonstration grounded in the simulated environment studied.
neurips-2022-explainability-via-causal-s.tldr: Causal Self-Talk trains reinforcement learning agents to model themselves through communication across time, supporting explanations and semantic control.

paragraphs: Vertical federated learning combines features held by different platforms to train a shared model. Those features can contain biases associated with sensitive attributes such as gender. FairVFL addresses fairness in this distributed setting, where methods requiring centralized storage of sensitive features are often unsuitable.

Platforms holding fairness-insensitive features first compute local representations. A server aggregates these into a unified representation for the prediction task. That representation is sent to platforms holding sensitive features, where adversarial learning is used to remove inherited bias. This arrangement lets distributed sensitive information contribute to fairness training without requiring its centralized storage.

Sending a unified representation between platforms also creates a privacy concern that the framework explicitly addresses. Before sharing it with the sensitive-feature platforms, FairVFL applies contrastive adversarial learning at the server to remove private information. Experiments on three real-world datasets report improved model fairness with user privacy well protected. The contribution is a coordinated representation-learning process that addresses both fairness and privacy within the distributed feature arrangement.
neurips-2022-fairvfl-a-fair-vertical-fed.tldr: FairVFL combines distributed representations and adversarial learning to improve fairness while protecting privacy in vertical federated learning.

paragraphs: A dataset and prediction task can admit several models with nearly equal predictive performance. This paper examines what that model indeterminacy means for explanations, which are commonly generated for a single fixed model. The central question is whether equally successful models also provide similar accounts of their decisions.

The authors show that model indeterminacy can produce explanatory multiplicity: different explanations across alternative models. Large differences can appear in explanations for a particular input even when aggregate test performance is very similar. They also find that predictive multiplicity and epistemic uncertainty are unreliable indicators of explanatory multiplicity, so those quantities cannot simply stand in for checking explanation variation.

The empirical investigation studies Shapley-value-based explanations on three risk assessment datasets. Results indicate that alternative models can yield inconsistent and even contradictory explanations in practice. This matters when interpreting a local explanation as a stable account of a decision: similar overall predictive quality does not establish that the explanation would remain similar under another comparably performing model.
neurips-2022-implications-of-model-indet.tldr: Models with similar predictive performance can give conflicting local explanations, and prediction uncertainty does not reliably reveal that variation.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equation models compute their transformations by solving differential equations. This paper proposes NesterovNODEs, whose layers solve second-order equations arising as a continuous limit of Nesterov's accelerated gradient method. It also introduces a generalized version, GNesterovNODEs, aimed at reducing the work needed by the equation solvers.

The approach draws on the accelerated method's O(1/k²) convergence rate. Its computational target is the number of function evaluations required to solve the differential equations, which affects both training and inference. The authors also prove that the adjoint state of a GNesterovNODE satisfies an equation of the same generalized form. This extends the acceleration mechanism to the backward solver as well as the forward solver.

Experiments cover point-cloud separation, image classification, and sequence modeling. Across the reported experiments, GNesterovNODEs use significantly fewer function evaluations than NODEs while achieving better accuracy. These findings support the proposed dynamics as a way to make continuous-depth models more computationally efficient, with the adjoint result helping the approach address the cost of training as well as prediction.
neurips-2022-improving-neural-ordinary-d.tldr: Nesterov-inspired neural differential equations reduce solver evaluations and improve accuracy across the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Collaborative filtering can confuse item popularity with user preference, pushing recommendations toward frequently encountered items. The paper argues that existing debiasing methods often trade performance on popular items against performance on less popular ones. It introduces BC Loss to reduce popularity bias while improving the learned representations of both groups.

BC Loss adds a bias-aware margin to a contrastive objective. The margin is quantitatively adjusted to the bias level of each user-item interaction. The authors analyze its geometry, visualize the representations, and provide a theoretical result supporting improved representations for both popular and less popular items. The mechanism encourages similar users or items to form compact groups while separating dissimilar ones.

The authors use BC Loss to train two high-performing collaborative-filtering models on six benchmark datasets. It outperforms the evaluated debiasing and non-debiasing methods across several settings, including balanced and imbalanced tests, temporal splits, and separate popular-item and less-popular-item evaluations. Based on these theoretical and empirical results, they advocate using BC Loss as a general recommendation objective as well as a debiasing method.
neurips-2022-incorporating-bias-aware-ma.tldr: BC Loss adjusts contrastive margins to interaction bias, improving recommendations for both popular and less popular items in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Federated learning can expose information through shared gradient updates even when the underlying training examples are not directly shared. Earlier reconstruction attacks had mainly demonstrated success on images. LAMP addresses text, where those methods do not transfer directly, and shows that original textual inputs can be reconstructed from gradients.

The attack combines two ideas. An auxiliary language model assigns probabilities to candidate text, guiding the search toward more natural language. The optimization alternates between continuous adjustments to embeddings and discrete transformations of the text. The continuous steps reduce reconstruction loss, while the discrete changes help the search avoid local minima.

Experiments report reconstruction of five times as many bigrams and subsequences that are 23% longer on average than prior work. The authors also report the first recovery of textual-model inputs from batches larger than one. These findings indicate that text-model gradients can reveal more information than earlier attacks demonstrated. The contribution is both a stronger reconstruction method and empirical evidence that keeping raw text local does not by itself prevent information leakage through updates.
neurips-2022-lamp-extracting-text-from-g.tldr: LAMP combines language-model guidance with continuous and discrete optimization to reconstruct text from shared gradients more effectively.

paragraphs: The neural tangent kernel, or NTK, is a mathematical tool for studying neural-network training. Earlier spectral analyses considered networks with at least one layer containing a number of neurons proportional to the number of training examples. This paper asks whether useful NTK conditioning can also hold when layer widths grow more slowly than the dataset.

The main technical result is a lower bound on the smallest NTK eigenvalue for deep networks in a minimally over-parameterized regime. Up to logarithmic factors, the parameter count scales as Ω(N), while the number of neurons can be as small as Ω(√N), where N is the number of training samples. The result answers the conditioning question affirmatively in the setup studied.

The authors apply this spectral bound to obtain results on memorization capacity and gradient-descent optimization. This matters because theoretical explanations of successful training need not always depend on layers as wide as the dataset. The contribution extends NTK-based guarantees into a narrower-network regime while retaining enough total parameters relative to the number of samples.
neurips-2022-memorization-and-optimizati.tldr: New NTK spectral bounds support memorization and optimization guarantees for deep networks with sublinear widths and near-linear parameter counts.

paragraphs: This paper addresses the limited ability of fixed neural policies to keep learning beyond their training curriculum. Inspired by persistent biological synaptic plasticity, it proposes networks whose weights remain dynamic. Their modifications depend on both the current synaptic state and feedback from actions and rewards.

The resulting system, Meta-Optimized Dynamical Synapses, or MetODS, uses meta-reinforcement learning to learn control rules for these changing connections. The network's current state helps determine how it changes next, making adaptation part of the policy's operation. This gives the agent a learned mechanism for responding to experience rather than relying solely on a fixed configuration produced during training.

The authors report that a single layer with dynamic synapses can perform one-shot learning, transfer navigation principles to unseen environments, and learn adaptive motor policies. The model compares favorably with previous meta-reinforcement learning approaches in the reported work. These findings support dynamic synapses as a mechanism for efficient adaptation across the studied tasks, connecting learned weight changes to flexible behavior.
neurips-2022-meta-reinforcement-learning.tldr: MetODS learns rules for changing its own synapses, enabling rapid adaptation in the reported navigation and motor-control tasks.

paragraphs: Color-based adversarial attacks alter meaningful image colors to make neural networks produce incorrect outputs. Their challenge is to preserve a natural-looking image while allowing enough freedom to create effective attacks. This paper argues that existing approaches restrict that freedom too much, limiting their performance against black-box models.

Natural Color Fool, or NCF, guides image changes using realistic color distributions sampled from a publicly available dataset. It combines that guidance with neighborhood search and initialization resets to optimize the attack. The intended benefit is stronger transferability of adversarial examples while preserving image quality, using realistic color distributions to guide the search.

Experiments and visualizations support the method's effectiveness. The authors report average improvements over state-of-the-art approaches ranging from 15.0% to 32.9% when fooling normally trained models and from 10.0% to 25.3% when evading defenses. These results show that realistic color guidance can coexist with stronger attacks in the evaluated settings. The contribution is an attack design that treats natural appearance and effective black-box transfer as compatible goals.
neurips-2022-natural-color-fool-towards-.tldr: Natural Color Fool uses realistic color distributions and search refinements to improve black-box adversarial attacks while preserving image quality.

paragraphs: Neural Attentive Circuits aim to combine broad applicability with modular computation. Modular networks can offer efficient adaptation and robustness, but often require assumptions about the data domain. NACs jointly learn what their modules do and how those modules connect sparsely, without using domain knowledge.

The architecture contains two systems trained together end to end: one determines the module configuration, and the other executes it on an input. On the NLVR2 visual-language reasoning dataset, the authors qualitatively observe diverse, meaningful configurations learned without extra supervision. This demonstrates that module organization can emerge as part of training rather than being specified for the task.

Quantitatively, NACs improve low-shot adaptation over a strong non-modular baseline by about 10 percent on CIFAR and CUB, and out-of-distribution robustness by about 2.5 percent on Tiny ImageNet-R. They can also achieve an eightfold inference speedup with less than a 3 percent performance loss. Competitive results on point clouds, symbolic processing, and text classification from ASCII bytes further support the architecture's applicability across different data modalities.
neurips-2022-neural-attentive-circuits-9.tldr: Neural Attentive Circuits learn sparse modular architectures that improve adaptation, robustness, and inference efficiency in the reported evaluations.

paragraphs: Deep graph convolutional networks can be difficult to train for several reasons, including overly similar node representations, compressed information, vanishing gradients, and overfitting. This paper focuses on gradient flow, which the authors argue has received less attention than other explanations. They hypothesize that improving it can make ordinary deep GCNs substantially more trainable.

The authors introduce two interventions. First, they derive a topology-aware initialization based on isometry principles, arguing that simply applying Glorot initialization is not optimal for GCNs. Second, they dynamically add skip connections using gradient information from each layer during training. These connections are introduced adaptively when the observed gradient flow indicates a need.

Experiments across multiple datasets show improved gradient flow and substantially better performance for deep vanilla GCNs. The resulting models compete with and outperform many sophisticated state-of-the-art methods in the evaluations. The findings support gradient flow as a productive target for improving deep graph networks, showing that initialization and adaptive connectivity can unlock stronger performance from an otherwise basic architecture.
neurips-2022-old-can-be-gold-better-grad.tldr: Topology-aware initialization and gradient-guided skip connections substantially improve the training and performance of deep vanilla GCNs.

paragraphs: A stochastic differential equation can describe optimization as a continuous trajectory while retaining the randomness of stochastic training. Such approximations had already been useful for studying stochastic gradient descent. This paper develops rigorously justified counterparts for the adaptive optimizers RMSprop and Adam, filling a gap identified by the authors.

The contribution includes theoretical guarantees for the correctness of these approximations and experimental evidence that they apply to common large-scale vision and language settings. Preserving stochasticity matters to the purpose of the model: the continuous description is intended to represent the noisy optimization process, rather than only a deterministic path through the parameters.

A practical outcome is a square-root scaling rule for adjusting optimization hyperparameters when batch size changes. The authors derive this rule for RMSprop and Adam and validate it empirically in deep learning settings. The work therefore connects a mathematical description of adaptive optimization to a concrete training decision: how to adjust optimizer settings when changing the amount of data processed in each batch.
neurips-2022-on-the-sdes-and-scaling-rul.tldr: Rigorous stochastic differential equation approximations for Adam and RMSprop yield empirically validated square-root batch-size scaling rules.

paragraphs: Some difficult inputs require more inference computation than easier ones. This paper studies equilibrium models as a broader class of architectures that can exploit repeated computation, reproducing the performance of earlier depth-wise recurrent approaches. It investigates which property is associated with better generalization when harder examples need additional iterations.

The central property is path independence: given enough computation, the system reaches the same attractor or limit cycle regardless of its initialization. Stronger generalization to harder examples correlates strongly with this property. The authors also perform interventions: promoting path independence improves generalization to harder instances, while penalizing it degrades that ability.

The relationship appears at the level of individual examples as well. For equilibrium models with good in-distribution performance, path independence on out-of-distribution inputs correlates strongly with accuracy. These results make path independence a useful lens for understanding when extra inference computation helps. The evidence combines correlations with experimental interventions, supporting the property as a meaningful design consideration without establishing that it guarantees correct answers on every difficult input.
neurips-2022-path-independent-equilibriu.tldr: Path independence is strongly associated with better use of extra inference computation, and promoting it improves generalization in experiments.

paragraphs: This paper studies reinforcement learning with several agents acting simultaneously in the same environment and sharing their experience. Under Thompson sampling, each agent independently samples a possible environment from a shared posterior and follows its corresponding optimal policy. The shared data supports learning, while independent samples encourage diverse exploration.

For finite-horizon episodic learning, each agent samples at the start of an episode. The authors prove a per-agent regret bound of Õ(HS√(AT/n)), where H is episode length, S the number of states, A the number of actions, T the number of episodes, and n the number of agents. Regret measures the learning cost relative to the relevant optimal behavior.

For infinite-horizon learning evaluated by long-run average reward, the method uses a doubling-horizon schedule because episodes provide no natural update boundaries. The reported regret bound is Õ(DS√(ATn)), with D denoting the environment's diameter and T the number of timesteps. Across both settings, per-agent regret decreases at the stated optimal rate of Θ(1/√n), giving a theoretical account of how cooperation improves learning.
neurips-2022-society-of-agents-regret-bo.tldr: Concurrent Thompson sampling receives regret guarantees showing an optimal inverse-square-root reduction in per-agent regret as more agents cooperate.

paragraphs: The paper studies an online decision problem in which an algorithm selects B options from N available options each round. Its cost is the lowest cost among those selected. Performance is compared with the single best option chosen in hindsight, so the central question is how a larger selection budget improves regret against that benchmark.

The proposed Follow the Perturbed Multiple Leaders algorithm achieves expected regret O(T^(1/(B+1)) · ln(N)^(B/(B+1))) over T rounds. Increasing B reduces the exponent governing growth with time. This makes the resource trade-off explicit: the algorithm can obtain a better regret bound by selecting more options each round under the minimum-cost rule.

The authors show that some methods using conventional regret minimizers can instead use this algorithm as a subroutine. They apply the idea to online submodular maximization with full and semi-bandit feedback and evaluate the resulting algorithms on online black-box hyperparameter optimization. They also derive linear-programming algorithms that exchange stronger oracles for fewer oracle calls, extending the same resource-versus-iteration theme.
neurips-2022-trading-off-resource-budget.tldr: Selecting more options per round improves regret against the best single option, with applications to online optimization and linear programming.

paragraphs: Variable Experience Rollout, or VER, improves the throughput of batched on-policy reinforcement learning when environments take very different times to generate experience. It retains on-policy data while removing synchronization points, combining characteristics of synchronous and asynchronous training. The method supports many GPUs, potentially distributed across multiple machines.

In simulated navigation, VER achieves 1.6–2 times the speed of DD-PPO with similar sample efficiency. For mobile manipulation, it reports 2.5 times the speed on one GPU and 2.7 times on eight GPUs. Compared with SampleFactory, it matches single-GPU speed and reaches a 1.7-fold speedup on eight GPUs, with better sample efficiency.

The authors use the additional throughput to train chained rearrangement skills and observe an unexpected transfer behavior. A picking skill trained with the robot always near a table can navigate and then pick objects in new environments with 50% success, provided base movement belongs to its action space. This is a specific out-of-distribution result: navigation emerges despite not being needed during that skill's training.
neurips-2022-ver-scaling-on-policy-rl-le.tldr: VER accelerates on-policy reinforcement learning, and a trained picking skill exhibits unexpected navigation ability in new environments.
